title: Mid-day meal workers: cooking for twelve crore children
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The cooks and helpers of PM POSHAN are among the lowest paid workers in the country.
body:
Every school day, a hot cooked meal is served to children in government and government-aided schools across India. The scheme began as the National Programme of Nutritional Support to Primary Education in 1995 and is now called **PM POSHAN**. It reaches children in the order of twelve crore, a figure that the Government's own scheme pages put at about 11.80 crore children in about 11.20 lakh schools. Behind every one of those meals is a cook, and most of the cooks are women who are paid an amount that the law does not even call a wage. This post looks at how the scheme works, who runs its kitchens, what they earn, and what BMS and its Mid-Day Meal workers' federation are asking for.

## A scheme with a long history

The idea of feeding children at school is older than the Republic. According to the Ministry of Education's scheme history, a mid-day meal programme began in the Madras Municipal Corporation as far back as 1925. By the mid-1980s Gujarat, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Pondicherry had universalised cooked meals using their own resources, and by 1990-91 twelve States were running some form of programme.

The national programme started on **15 August 1995** as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme in 2,408 blocks, and it reached all blocks by 1997-98. It was extended to all government, local body and aided primary and upper primary schools from 1 April 2008. In 2021 the Union Cabinet approved the scheme under its present name for the five years 2021-22 to 2025-26. The Ministry describes it as a rights-based scheme under the National Food Security Act, 2013, which means that an eligible child is entitled to the meal, or to a food security allowance where a meal cannot be served.

## What the scheme covers

PM POSHAN covers children in Classes I to VIII, and the 2021 approval added pre-primary or Balvatika children in government and government-aided primary schools. The approved financial plan for 2021-22 to 2025-26 runs to about Rs 1,30,794.90 crore in total. Of this, the Centre's share is about Rs 54,061.73 crore, the States' and Union Territories' share about Rs 31,733.17 crore, and a further cost of about Rs 45,000 crore for food grains is met by the Centre. Social audits were made mandatory in all districts, and the scheme encourages local sourcing, school nutrition gardens and community contributions such as Tithi Bhojan.

The money is divided into several heads. For cooking cost, which covers ingredients and fuel, the rate from 1 April 2020 was Rs 4.97 per child per day for primary classes and Rs 7.45 for upper primary classes. Food grains, transport and monitoring are funded by the Centre. The honorarium of cooks and helpers is funded jointly, and States are free to add to it from their own budgets.

## Who cooks

The meal is prepared by **cook-cum-helpers**, mostly women from the neighbourhood of the school. Staffing norms fixed in 2009 provide for one cook-cum-helper for up to 25 students, two for 26 to 100 students, and one more for every additional 100. The Ministry's history records that over 25.25 lakh cook-cum-helpers were engaged by States and Union Territories in 2016-17, and a recent news report quotes unions as saying that nearly 25 lakh work in rural areas alone. They work for about five hours a day according to that report, though anyone who has seen a school kitchen knows that preparation starts well before the first child arrives.

The work is physically heavy. Cooks handle large vessels of rice, dal and vegetables over a fire or a gas stove, wash the utensils, clean the kitchen and serve the children. In its memorandum to the Union Education Minister, BMS has also pointed out that these workers are frequently given duties that have nothing to do with the meal, such as sweeping the school, acting as watchman or running errands in the office.

## What they earn

Cook-cum-helpers are paid an **honorarium**, not a wage. The central norm, in force since 1 December 2009, is **Rs 1,000 per month, paid for ten months a year**. A reply given in the Lok Sabha confirms that the honorarium remains Rs 1,000 a month for ten months, with a summer-vacation honorarium paid in drought-affected areas that State governments notify.

It is worth doing the arithmetic. Ten months at Rs 1,000 is Rs 10,000 for the year, which is less than Rs 850 for each month if it is spread over twelve. Unions point out that this is far below the minimum wage notified for unskilled work. Some States top up the central amount from their own funds, so what a cook actually receives depends on where she lives. A page on the West Bengal government's PM POSHAN portal, for instance, describes a Rs 2,000 monthly honorarium from 1 April 2024 in which the Centre contributes Rs 600 and the State pays the rest. But the central norm itself has stayed at Rs 1,000 for years, and CITU has said it is unchanged since 2009.

Because the payment is an honorarium for a scheme, the workers are not treated as employees. BMS argues that this is exactly why they miss the health and social security benefits that labour laws give to workers.

## The long-standing demand for recognition

The demand is not new. At the 45th Indian Labour Conference, held on 17-18 May 2013, the tripartite body recommended that scheme workers should be recognised as workers and paid minimum wages. The action-taken report prepared for the 46th session in 2015 records that the ministries concerned replied that anganwadi workers and mid-day meal cook-cum-helpers could not be treated as workers. Unions say the Government assured an increase in remuneration at the 2013 conference, and that the increase has not followed.

## BMS and mid-day meal workers

BMS works among these workers through the **Akhil Bharatiya Mid-Day Meal Karmachari Mahasangh**, which it describes as one of its industrial units. On 1 July 2025 the Mahasangh held demonstrations at about 400 places across the country to draw attention to the workers' problems. In early September 2025 a BMS delegation led by All-India Organising Secretary B. Surendran and All-India Secretary Ashok Shukla met Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and submitted a memorandum, which was also sent to the Prime Minister.

According to BMS's own account of the meeting, the memorandum asked for a monthly honorarium of Rs 10,000 and drew attention to low wages, inadequate health facilities, harassment by supervisory staff, and delays in payment to self-help groups that run the scheme in some States, such as Madhya Pradesh. It also complained that some district officials do not supply enough ration. BMS reports that the Minister promised to write to the Finance Minister about raising monthly wages and to arrange a meeting with officials.

The wider list of demands that unions put forward includes:

- Recognition as **workers**, with at least the minimum wage.
- Payment for **twelve months** instead of ten.
- **ESI, provident fund** and pension.
- Safe cooking arrangements, with LPG in place of firewood, and accident insurance.
- Regular and timely payment, without months of delay.

## What remains to be done

News reports in late 2025 said that the Department of School Education and Literacy had told the States that PM POSHAN would be restructured and had asked them for suggestions. The scheme's current approval period runs only to 2025-26, so the question of what the next phase pays its cooks is a live one. The reports did not mention any figure or commitment on honorarium.

For workers and for readers, the points to watch are plain. Will the next approval raise the central honorarium, which has been fixed for so long? Will the honorarium be paid for twelve months? Will payment be regular, through direct bank transfer? And will the Centre and the States settle whether these cooks, who feed more than eleven crore children, are to be counted as workers at all?

## Closing

When we ask how a child learns on a full stomach, the answer begins in a kitchen where somebody is awake before dawn. A scheme that is intended to make children healthy cannot reasonably rest on the unpaid margins of the women who cook the food. Recognition, a living income and security for these workers are not extras. They are part of what it takes to run the scheme well.
